paper_metadata.title: Quantum Monte Carlo Simulations for predicting electron-positron pair production via the linear Breit-Wheeler process

summary: This paper presents a gate-based quantum Monte Carlo / iterative quantum amplitude estimation workflow for linear Breit-Wheeler pair production, using a second-degree polynomial approximation of the cross-section and 6144 shots in the reported simulations. In ideal simulation, the authors report mean percentage errors of 0.156% (Qiskit initialization), 0.115% (FSL), and 0.167% (variational), corresponding to about 99.8% accuracy versus theory; on IonQ Forte Enterprise, they report about 87% mean accuracy and up to 90% accuracy relative to theoretical predictions.

experiments.description: Quantum Monte Carlo / iterative quantum amplitude estimation for predicting electron-positron pair production in the linear Breit-Wheeler process, evaluated in ideal simulation with three state-preparation methods (Qiskit native initialization, variational initialization, Fourier Series Loader).

algorithm.variant: Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) with Grover-style amplitude amplification
algorithm.ansatz: Variational CNOT-Ry ring ansatz for state preparation; Fourier Series Loader for alternative initialization
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Iteratively checks whether target accuracy epsilon is satisfied
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Variational initialization used a parametric circuit; FSL coefficients computed classically and truncated; Qiskit native initialization used built-in state preparation

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Photon energy distribution encoded in the work register; pair-production probability embedded into an ancilla via controlled Ry rotations after polynomial approximation of the Breit-Wheeler cross-section
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate expected pair-production probability mu = E_X[p(X)] and convert to expected number of pairs N_pairs = N_int * mu
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Probability function scaled to [0,1] before ancilla rotation; no explicit penalty formulation

problem_instance.description: Head-on collision of two gamma-photon beams for linear Breit-Wheeler pair production; one beam monoenergetic, the other Gaussian-like

dataset_specification.description: Monoenergetic beam energy varied; Gaussian beam mean 6 MeV, sigma 1; skewness varied in one study

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Breit-Wheeler cross-section approximated by a second-degree polynomial; probability rescaled to [0,1]; Gaussian distribution discretized on a qubit grid
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Comparison against theoretical predictions and classical Monte Carlo; relative error reported across parameter sweeps; same number of queries/samples (6144) for classical and quantum Monte Carlo

implementation_details.classical_solver: NumPy random sampling for classical Monte Carlo baseline; SciPy curve_fit for polynomial fitting
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical fitting of Breit-Wheeler cross-section to a low-order polynomial; Fourier coefficients computed classically for FSL
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measured amplitudes converted back to pair-production probability and multiplied by number of interacting particles

speedup_claims.conditions: in principle for amplitude estimation; practical setup limited by polynomial approximation of the Breit-Wheeler cross-section
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the setup does not show the quadratic speedup in practice because of approximation error from polynomial embedding; quantum arithmetic would be too deep for NISQ devices.

speedup_claims.factor: better accuracy than classical Monte Carlo
speedup_claims.caveats: Improvement is in mean percentage error, not runtime; the best quantum mean error reported is 0.115% versus 0.191% classical.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Quadratic speedup claimed for amplitude estimation in principle; practical setup limited by polynomial approximation
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical Monte Carlo scales as O(1/epsilon^2) for sampling accuracy in the standard setting

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not established; ideal simulations use 6144 shots and compare state-preparation methods, but no practical resource crossover is demonstrated.
limiting_factors: Only ideal/emulated simulation results are reported here
Speedup is only theoretical quadratic amplitude-estimation speedup
Accuracy is limited by polynomial approximation and state preparation
No meaningful classical-vs-quantum runtime advantage is shown

notes: hardware.type inferred as simulator_other because the paper reports ideal simulations using Qiskit and separately reports a real QPU experiment; this experiment is the ideal simulator comparison.
num_qubits not explicitly given for the ideal-simulator sweep; only work-register sizes of 4, 6, and 8 qubits are reported in the figures, so total qubits are inferred as not fully specified.
The paper reports high numerical accuracy in simulation, but does not demonstrate practical quantum advantage over classical methods.

experiments.description: Quantum Monte Carlo / IQAE on IonQ Forte Enterprise trapped-ion QPU for linear Breit-Wheeler pair production, using reduced-qubit state preparation (FSL and variational initialization).

algorithm.variant: Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) on hardware
algorithm.ansatz: Variational CNOT-Ry ring ansatz; Fourier Series Loader
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Iterative amplitude estimation until target accuracy is met
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Parametric circuit for variational initialization; FSL coefficients computed classically

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Three-qubit work register encodes the photon energy distribution; polynomial approximation of the Breit-Wheeler cross-section embedded into ancilla rotations
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate expected pair-production probability and expected number of pairs for head-on photon collisions
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Probability scaled to [0,1] before controlled Ry embedding

problem_instance.description: Head-on collision of two photon beams on a trapped-ion quantum computer; one beam monoenergetic, the other Gaussian-like

dataset_specification.description: Monoenergetic beam energies 3, 6, and 9 MeV; Gaussian beam mean 6 MeV, sigma 1

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Cross-section approximated by a second-degree polynomial; state preparation reduced to three qubits to minimize cost
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Six simulations with 6144 shots; results compared to ideal cloud-service simulations and theoretical predictions; relative error reported

implementation_details.classical_solver: SciPy curve_fit; local post-processing of JSON results
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical polynomial fitting of the Breit-Wheeler cross-section; classical computation of Fourier coefficients for FSL
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Downloaded QPU results in JSON format and post-processed locally to estimate pair counts

speedup_claims.conditions: in principle for amplitude estimation on NISQ hardware
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper does not report a direct runtime speedup on hardware; it reports feasibility and accuracy on IonQ Forte Enterprise.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Quadratic speedup claimed in principle for amplitude estimation

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: 3-qubit work register, 6144 shots, IonQ Forte Enterprise trapped-ion QPU; no resource crossover analysis is provided.
limiting_factors: No runtime or cost advantage over classical Monte Carlo is shown
Quadratic amplitude-estimation advantage is not realized in practice
Polynomial approximation and state preparation dominate the error budget

notes: The paper explicitly reports use of IonQ Forte Enterprise and a three-qubit work register.
Circuit depth is not reported; only the use of a reduced-qubit circuit and 6144 shots is stated.
The paper reports up to 90% accuracy on IonQ Forte Enterprise and a mean accuracy of 87% relative to theory, but no classical-vs-quantum advantage is demonstrated.
